title: Food & Cooking · Episode 2
chapters: Cooking by degrees: the science of precise temperature

units.t: Food & Cooking. Episode two.
In this episode: Food safety at home, Cooking by degrees: the science of precise temperature and Kitchen myths, busted.
Part one. Food safety at home.
Australians get food poisoning millions of times a year, and much of it starts in home kitchens.
A few habits prevent most of it.
Bacteria and the danger zone.
Food Standards Australia New Zealand estimates Australians have around 4 to 5 million cases of food poisoning each year, with tens of thousands of hospitalisations.
Many are never diagnosed and are dismissed as a '24-hour bug'.
Causes include Campylobacter, Salmonella, Listeria, toxin-producing E.
coli and norovirus.
Pregnant women, babies, young children, older people and anyone with a weakened immune system face a higher risk, especially from soft cheeses, deli meats and raw eggs.
Most bacteria multiply fastest between 5 degrees and 60 degrees, the danger zone, and some can double every 20 minutes or so.
Keep the fridge at 5 degrees or below, ideally 3 to 4 degrees, the freezer at about minus 18 degrees, and hot food above 60 degrees.
Some bacteria make toxins that cooking doesn't destroy, so prevention matters more than reheating.
Time rules and leftovers.
The 2-hour/4-hour rule guides ready-to-eat food that has been left out.
It counts the total time between 5 degrees and 60 degrees.
Under 2 hours, use it or refrigerate it.
Between 2 and 4 hours, use it straight away.
Over 4 hours, throw it out.
On a hot Australian day, bring an esky with ice bricks to picnics and barbecues.
Leftovers are safe if handled well.
Refrigerate cooked food once it stops steaming, and divide large batches into shallow containers so they cool faster.
Eat within 2 to 3 days or freeze.
Reheat until steaming hot throughout, ideally 75 degrees, and only once.
Rice needs extra care: spores of Bacillus cereus survive cooking and produce toxins if rice sits at room temperature, so cool and refrigerate it quickly.
Raw meat, heat and eggs.
Cross-contamination spreads bacteria from raw meat, poultry or seafood to food that won't be cooked again.
Store raw meat in sealed containers on the bottom shelf.
Use separate boards for raw meat and salads, or wash boards and knives in hot soapy water between uses.
Don't wash raw chicken: splashing spreads Campylobacter around the kitchen, and cooking kills it anyway.
Cook chicken, mince, sausages, burgers and rolled or stuffed meats to 75 degrees in the thickest part, because mincing and rolling mix surface bacteria inside.
Dishes with raw or lightly cooked eggs, such as homemade mayonnaise, aioli and eggnog, are a leading cause of Salmonella outbreaks in Australia.
Use pasteurised egg products and keep raw-egg sauces in the fridge for no more than a day.
Symptoms and getting help.
Food poisoning usually causes nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, stomach cramps and sometimes fever, headache or aches.
Symptoms can start within a few hours of eating or take several days, depending on the cause; Listeria can take weeks.
That means the last meal you ate isn't always the culprit.
Most cases pass within a few days.
The main priority is fluids: sip water or oral rehydration solution from a pharmacy.
See a doctor if you have blood in your stool, signs of dehydration such as dizziness or very little urine, a high fever, or symptoms lasting more than a few days.
Seek help early if you are in a high-risk group.
Four everyday habits.
Most home food poisoning can be prevented with four habits.
Clean: wash hands before cooking and after handling raw meat, and keep benches, boards and tea towels clean.
Chill: refrigerate food promptly and check your fridge with a cheap thermometer.
Separate: keep raw and ready-to-eat foods apart.
Cook: cook high-risk foods thoroughly.
Also avoid cooking for others while you have vomiting or diarrhoea, and for at least 48 hours after symptoms stop.
Don't use cracked or dirty eggs.
When in doubt, throw it out: a smell test can't detect many harmful bacteria.
This is general information, not medical advice.
The key idea: Food poisoning is common in Australia, and bacteria multiply fastest between 5 degrees and 60 degrees.
Part two. Cooking by degrees: the science of precise temperature.
A few degrees can turn silky meat into shoe leather.
Understanding exactly what heat does to proteins explains sous vide, perfect eggs and why chefs swear by thermometers.
Cooking is protein chemistry.
Proteins are long chains folded into specific shapes.
Heat makes them vibrate until the weak bonds holding their shape give way.
They unfold, denaturation, then tangle with their neighbours, coagulation.
That is what turns runny egg white solid and translucent prawn flesh firm and opaque.
The crucial detail is that different proteins set at different temperatures.
In an egg, ovotransferrin starts setting near 62 degrees, the yolk thickens around 65, and ovalbumin needs close to 80.
Hold an egg at 63 to 65 degrees for about an hour and you get a custard-like yolk and a barely set white, as in Japanese onsen tamago, cooked in hot springs.
Boiling water at 100 degrees overshoots everything.
What happens inside meat.
Meat is mostly water held inside muscle proteins and wrapped in connective tissue made largely of collagen.
The muscle protein myosin begins to set at around 50 degrees, so the meat firms but stays juicy.
That is roughly the rare range.
Through the 60s, other proteins, including actin at about 66 degrees or above, contract and squeeze out moisture, and the meat turns noticeably drier.
Collagen behaves differently.
It shrinks at around 60 degrees, but given enough time at higher temperatures it slowly breaks down into gelatine.
That gives braised meat its silky, falling-apart texture.
Hence the cook's dilemma: tender cuts want low temperatures, while tough, collagen-rich cuts need long cooking.
Why sous vide works.
Sous vide is French for 'under vacuum'.
Food is sealed in a bag and cooked in a water bath held at an exact temperature.
Its culinary use is usually traced to 1974, when chef Georges Pralus used it for foie gras, which lost far less fat under gentle heat.
Food scientist Bruno Goussault later trained chefs in it.
Home circulators became affordable in the 2010s.
Water carries heat much faster than air, which is why you can briefly put a hand in a 200 degree oven but not in boiling water.
Set the bath to 56 degrees for medium-rare steak and the food can never get hotter.
It cooks evenly from edge to centre, with no grey band.
Cooks then add a quick, hot sear for browning.
Time as well as temperature.
Food safety guidance usually gives one number, such as cooking poultry until the centre reaches 75 degrees, which kills bacteria like Salmonella almost instantly.
But bacterial death really depends on temperature and time together.
At lower temperatures bacteria still die, just more slowly.
Food scientists have published tables showing that holding food at a lower temperature for long enough achieves the same reduction as a brief moment at a higher one.
That is how sous vide cooks can safely serve juicier chicken.
These methods need accurate equipment, correct holding times and an understanding of the science.
For everyday home cooking, follow the official temperature guidance and check with a probe thermometer.
The risks and the thermometer.
Precise low temperature cooking has risks that conventional cooking avoids.
In a sealed, airless bag, bacteria that thrive without oxygen, such as Clostridium botulinum, can become a hazard if food is held too long at too low a temperature or cooled slowly afterwards.
Cooking below about 55 degrees for long periods is particularly risky.
Eat cooked food promptly, or chill it quickly in iced water and refrigerate it.
Pregnant people, young children, older adults and those with weakened immunity are generally advised to avoid lightly cooked meat, fish and eggs.
For any cook, the best tool is a probe thermometer.
Once you know the internal temperature, you are no longer guessing, and dry chicken and overcooked steak become far rarer.
The key idea: Heat changes the shape of proteins, and each protein sets at its own temperature, often only a few degrees apart.
Part three. Kitchen myths, busted.
Searing seals in juices.
Alcohol burns off.
Oil stops pasta sticking.
These ideas get passed from cook to cook, and many of them are simply wrong.
Searing seals nothing.
The idea that searing ‘seals in the juices’ goes back to the German chemist Justus von Liebig in the mid-1800s and spread through cookbooks for a century.
Experiments have repeatedly shown it is wrong.
A seared crust is not waterproof, and seared meat loses about as much moisture as unseared meat cooked to the same internal temperature, sometimes more.
The sizzle in the pan is moisture boiling away.
Searing is still worth doing, because the Maillard reaction creates deep browned flavour and appealing colour.
What keeps meat juicy is not overcooking it, which is why a thermometer matters far more than a dramatic sear.
Alcohol lingers in food.
Many people believe all the alcohol in wine or spirits disappears as soon as a dish is heated.
United States Department of Agriculture measurements show otherwise.
When alcohol was added to a boiling liquid and removed from the heat, most of it remained.
Flaming a dish left around three-quarters.
After 15 minutes of simmering, about 40 per cent was still there, and even after two and a half hours, around 5 per cent remained.
Alcohol and water evaporate together, so it never vanishes all at once.
The amounts per serve are usually small, but it matters for people who avoid alcohol completely for health, religious or recovery reasons, and for young children.
Pasta water myths.
Pouring oil into pasta water ‘to stop it sticking’ does almost nothing.
Oil and water do not mix, so the oil sits on the surface while the pasta tumbles below.
Pasta sticks in the first couple of minutes, when surface starch turns gluey.
Use plenty of water at a rolling boil and stir well early on.
Oil that coats drained pasta can make sauce slide off.
Save a cup of the starchy water instead, which helps sauces turn glossy.
Salt does not make water boil faster either.
Dissolved salt slightly raises the boiling point, but at cooking amounts the change is a fraction of a degree.
The real reason to salt is flavour: food absorbs salt as it cooks, seasoning it from within.
Microwaves and nutrients.
A popular belief says microwaves cook from the inside out.
In fact they penetrate only a centimetre or two into most foods, making water molecules jiggle and generate heat.
The centre of a large item warms as heat spreads inwards, just as in an oven, only from a thicker starting layer.
That is why recipes include standing time to let heat even out, and why stirring and rotating help avoid cold spots, which matter for food safety when reheating.
Another myth is that microwaving destroys nutrients.
Because cooking is quick and uses little water, microwaving vegetables often keeps water-soluble vitamins, such as vitamin C, as well as or better than boiling.
Dropped food and frozen food.
The five-second rule claims food is safe if picked up quickly.

In 2016, food scientist Donald Schaffner's team at Rutgers University contaminated surfaces including stainless steel, tile, wood and carpet with bacteria, then dropped watermelon, bread, buttered bread and gummy lollies.
Transfer could happen in under a second.
Longer contact meant more bacteria, but speed alone did not make food safe.
Moisture mattered most: watermelon picked up the most, dry lollies the least.
Fresh is not always better than frozen either.
Fresh vegetables can spend days in transport and your fridge, losing vitamins.
Frozen vegetables are blanched and frozen soon after harvest, and studies generally find similar nutrients.
Frozen peas, berries and spinach are cheap and waste less, while fresh often wins on texture and taste.
The key idea: Searing adds flavour but does not seal in juices; keeping meat juicy comes from not overcooking it.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why is the temperature range of 5 degrees to 60 degrees called the danger zone?
Answer. Bacteria multiply fastest in that range.
Question two. Why does an egg held at about 64 degrees have a custardy yolk and a soft white?
Answer. Each protein sets at its own temperature.
Question three. What actually keeps a steak juicy?
Answer. Not overcooking it.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
